utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. C-1141, they asked you somewhere towards the beginning of your testimony whether you had seen any paramilitary units when they arrived, when they had arrived from Serbia, whether you were there, and your answer was that you didn't see them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your answers when you used word "soldiers," as far as I understood you, you were in fact talking about local citizens who had put on uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in Hrvatska Dubica, there were no members of the JNA or anybody else from Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, as you say that relations in Hrvatska Dubica deteriorated in 1990, do you happen to know when in Croatia the HDZ party was formed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your opinion, was the HDZ a nationalistic party or was it a party of democratic option which could be deduced from its heading, its title?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but I'm a member of the Social Democratic Party, that's all I know, and as for the other one, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When the HDZ was established, did the local Serbs in Hrvatska Dubica have any party of their own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they form their own party?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Serbs in Croatia, and therefore, in Hrvatska Dubica as well, in 1990 to a large extent realised their political goals within this party which used to be the League of Communists of Croatia or, rather, the party I'm talking about is the SDP, that most of them at those first elections voted for the SDP party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it's not. Some -- some people voted or, rather, they already had -- in 1990, the parties had already been set up, the HDZ and the SDS and there were three of them, three parties, and the SDP was the third. And I was a member of the SDP. They asked me to be the president of the SDS but I refused. I turned that down, and that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear to me. Now, how long after the HDZ was the SDS formed in Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't tell you the day or the date but it was in 1990 sometime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understand. Now, is it true, [redacted], that as a child in World War II you were left an orphan without either parents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was left without a father.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The accused has used the witness's name instead of the pseudonym. I'd ask that it be redacted from the record and I'd ask Mr. Milosevic to be directed not to use his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm told that is so. Mr. Milosevic, don't use the name. You know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't notice having said it I said 1141 a moment ago. I addressed him in that way, but probably I misspoke and a slip of the tongue and said the name. I didn't do it on purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know how many Serbs left Hrvatska Dubica on the 2nd of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not leave Dubica. They would just leave during the day. That's what happened. They went to Bosanska Dubica. But in the morning -- actually, they would go to Bosanska Dubica in the evening and would return from Bosanska Dubica in the morning, back to their own homes. Whether they all went or not, I can't say. Whether the young people went off and the elderly people stayed to look after the homes, but that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why did they go away during the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they afraid of anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not quite clear to me. I'm not clear as to why they did so. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I have a piece of information here that tells me that on the 2nd of August, about 1.250 Serbs left their homes. Tell me, please, is it true that on that particular day in Hrvatska Dubica, 13 buses arrived belonging to members of the ZNG, the Croatian National Guard Corps and the police force, and that the column stretched from the centre of Dubica right up towards the Jesenovac area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you say in your statement that the Croats had organised themselves and were preparing for the threat that loomed over them. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So they weren't in jeopardy at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether somebody was afraid or not and for what reason I really can't say but they were not threatened. Everybody went about their own business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember an event when at the end of July 1991 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. members of the Croatian paramilitary units slaughtered Stevo Djuricic, a man who was 65 years old and he was a caretaker at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that, but I don't know what actually happened to him. I heard that he had been killed, but who killed him or what, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. C-1141, you say you know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he and not only him but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else did you hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was another person who was killed. Not only Djuricic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember when Stevo Vlatkovic, who disappeared without trace and we don't know his fate to this day, did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was captured in his own house and they found weapons in his house. Now, what happened to him after that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that another Serb, Petar Kojic, about 53 years of age, disappeared on the same day as Ugarkovic and ten days later his body was found in Gornji Bacin by a Croat, Milan Coric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether that was on the same day, I don't know, but yes, Pera Kojic was captured in a forest -- well, not a forest, actually, a wood, and he had a hunting rifle on him. Now, what happened to him afterwards, I really don't know, but I know that he's not around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it logical that when people are in the woods, they carry hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had a hunting rifle, yes. And it didn't belong to him either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I would like to ask the witness a few questions which I don't think can be asked in open session, just for a few minutes please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the local Serbs on the 18th of September, 1991, occupied Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just check here. Well, all right, I can't seem to find this in your statement just now. I did see it in your statement. If you say so, all right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me what you saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not important, never mind. Tell me this: What was the population structure in Hrvatska Dubica at the time that you're testifying about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mixed; Serbs, Croats, there were some Muslims too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 1 here of your statement or, rather, it's page 2, marked as page 2, last paragraph, or the penultimate paragraph in fact, it says -- and let me say that I received your statement only in English, so I'm going to quote in English and the interpreters will translate for you. It says the following: [In English] "When I left my village on the 16th of September (Saturday) the forces of SAO Krajina and other Serb paramilitaries were in the woods above Hrvatska Dubica. The Croatian defenders had already left the village but the Serb paramilitaries did not know that. However, they came to know of it very soon and occupied Hrvatska Dubica on Monday, 18th of September, 1991." [Interpretation] That means you say they occupied Hrvatska Dubica on the 18th of September, the Serbs, and that is what -- as it stands, and you say you didn't say that. Now, I'm asking you, how is it possible for them to occupy their own town and the houses and streets they lived in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are distorting some things. I did not say that they occupied it. I said that when the population withdrew, when the population left, when they withdrew, because in Dubica at that time there was the Croatian police there. There were no soldiers, no members of the army, I just saw the police. So when the bridge was blown up -- you see, you're distorting all this, because when the bridge was blown up, that's what happened. Several days later, people started to flee. Everybody fled. Now, what happened afterwards -- and you say that I said this was on the 16th. It was a Saturday. I don't remember the exact date, whether it was the 16th or the 17th, but it was a Saturday. Now, what happened afterwards, after that particular Saturday, I really don't know. I can't say. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. C-1141, please, I just read out the text of your statement because I know nothing about your town. All I can do is to read what you wrote down here, and I read it all word-for-word as it states in the statement. Now, does that mean that this is a mistake and that this observation was made by mistake? Because I haven't distorted or made up anything. I just read it out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, this word "occupy," why it says that, I don't know who could Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have occupied it. We had withdrawn. The place was left empty. Now, who came after that, I don't know. Whether it was the reservists or anybody else, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. That means it is not your statement and they did not occupy the place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my statement, and what I said I stand by now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And not -- you don't stand by what I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've read out some things which were probably not translated properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not translated properly you say, I see. Now, you just said that this was after the bridge had been blown up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me, please, who blew the bridge up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard -- I don't know who did it, but I heard that the bridge was blown up, it seems, by the Croatian police force or whoever was there. What their names were, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the paragraph before that, you say the following: [In English] "On 12th or 13th of September 1991 (Wednesday), the Croatians destroyed the bridge on Una River between Hrvatska Dubica and Bosanska Dubica as there was a possibility of JNA tanks coming over to this area."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. They were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So Croats or, rather, Croat paramilitaries had destroyed the bridge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Police did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Croatian police destroyed the bridge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then once the Croatian police destroyed the bridge, then the population started fleeing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. People continued living in Dubica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since you say they did not occupy, as is stated here, then I will put no more questions regarding this. Can you tell us whether before the 18th of September, 1991, there were -- there was some fighting in the wider area of Dubica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So since there was no fighting in that area, there was nobody who could attack or defend Dubica. The only violent event was the destruction of that bridge, as far as I understand it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me what else happened there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One couldn't reach Dubica. In the roads, there were roadblocks. There were trees knocked down and then there were guards or guard patrols on the road, in the hills. I don't know why it was there. I don't know the reason for that, but it was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that you're saying now that there were watchguards there, but was there any conflict there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm interested in. You told us that upon your return to Dubica, you saw a person called Momcilo Kovacevic who was -- who held a position, as far as I understood it, and you saw him putting posters up, posters warning that everybody looting houses would be punished.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I did see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that a lot of people had left Dubica, the houses were vacant, and as far as I understand it, this man was actually a policeman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did wear the uniform of the SAO police of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was putting up posters with warnings that those who loot houses would be punished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And I'm sorry I didn't bring with me one of those posters so that I could show it to you here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose that he and his colleagues wanted to protect the property of inhabitants of Hrvatska Dubica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as was said in those announcements, I believe that you're right. Now, whether they succeeded in actually implementing that, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you mention names of several commanders of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's reduce it to that one name that you mentioned. And that one name that you mentioned and this one person in fact is a resident of Hrvatska Dubica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, where was that man from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he was from. His name was Borojevic, and he got killed. He was a young man. I don't know his first name. He's gone now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see that you mention here -- and in fact you asked for a closed session in order to mention a name, and I wrote it down. You are saying that you were mentioning a commander of the guard near the firehouse station who was a local person, a local resident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's who I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. He was no commander at all. That man helped me to escape from the firehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You say on page 4, paragraph 3: "The commander of the guard --" so a third paragraph on page 4, you say that the commander of those guards, and then you mention his nickname and so on, and you say that he was a local resident from your town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was no commander at all. Yes, he was a local resident, and I suppose that he had something to do with those guards watching us in the firehouse. Now, what was his position, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. C-1141. All I'm doing is reading your statement out loud to you because you, in your statement, call him the commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The commander of the staff was Borojevic, and the staff was located in a different village, and all of them wore olive-drab uniforms or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "olive-drab uniforms," you are in fact referring to old JNA uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were reservists. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the JNA had camouflage combat uniforms. They in fact did not wear old uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these people, the reservists, in fact had those old uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the local people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, reservists. I don't know any other people other than them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So while you were there, you did not see anybody who came from outside to Hrvatska Dubica. Those were all locals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were locals there, yes, and there were several people whom I didn't know. I saw them but I didn't know them. And later I learned that they were from Bosanska Dubica. And as to who had brought them there and why they came there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are from Bosanska Dubica too as far as I understood it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosanska Dubica is just across the Una River; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was this bridge that was blown up by Croatian police between Bosanska/Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that it was destroyed on the Croatian side, and now I don't know who destroyed it. I heard that it was them, because nobody else had access there. The police guarded the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. C-1141. Now, tell me, please, do you have any information regarding how many Serb houses were looted after the 2nd August of 1991 when 1.250 Serbs, based on my information, left Dubica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that a single house was looted or set on fire at that time. All I know is that upon my return on the 2nd of October, 1991, from Ljubljana where I stayed with my brother, that there were burnt houses. I stayed there for 18 days, and I saw that 12 houses were burnt down. And later on, my house as well. After I left, my house was set on fire, the last. And I don't know about people looting houses. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, yes, I see that you don't know. All I'm trying is to extract what you do know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will say what I do know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that during July of 1991 in -- dynamite was thrown on several Serb houses in and around Dubica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Mateljak Tomislav?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's a Croat, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that in his car a large amount of dynamite and weapons was found, in his car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never heard about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend a meeting of residents of Dubica, both Serbs and Croats, which was called in order to calm down tensions, inter-ethnic tensions, and to calm down the situation and in order to organise jointly and protect themselves from any possible attacks and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this meeting but I did not attend it. I did not attend it, but the meeting was held. I don't know in which building it was held either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that on the 19th of October, 1991, in Zelenik forest, not far from Hrvatska Dubica, four persons were killed, all of them Serbs: Zoran Tatic, 34 years old; Rajko Burazor, 35 years old; Mladen Tomic, born in 1965; and Nenad Mitrovic, 30 years old. Did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But they encountered a mine in their vehicle, and there were two older men in that vehicle and one middle-aged man as well. They were all from that town. And it didn't happen in the town itself but as they were leaving town, they took with them two other men, and as they were leaving down, they ran into a mine and all of them were blown up. Yes, that's what I heard and that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You are mostly describing things that you had heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify your evidence regarding the firehouse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many hours did you spend in the firehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 9.00 in the morning until 5.30 or 6.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have a watch on me, but around that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that you were called and you asked to go home to get some clothing, and then after that, you escaped in the hills; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, you don't know what was going on in the firehouse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The elderly remained at the firehouse that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those who were with you up until the moment you left the place remained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know, therefore, whether anybody else left the firehouse just like you did and the other ten people that you mentioned or whether they were remained there in the firehouse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I left, they remained in the firehouse. However, during the night, and there are some living witnesses who can testify to this, three or four persons that were taken out alive, out of them only one old lady died. So three or four people were taken out alive, three or four people who remained after me. And as to who took them out, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was going to ask you. How do you know how those people perished, whether they perished afterwards, on that occasion? You basically don't know what went on afterwards. You left the firehouse at 6.00 p.m. and don't know what happened afterwards because you fled.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about possible motives.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clarify this. You were asked, on the last day of your testimony, about being arrested a few days later on and being taken to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. police station and being kept there for two days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't after a couple of days. You are putting it wrongly. Why don't you ask me about things that I experienced and saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you, when did the police arrest you after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Sunday, in the evening, upon my escape from the firehouse. Once I escaped, I fled into the hills to my friend's place. I spent the night there, and then a transfer was organised to transfer me from Hrvatska Dubica to Bosnia, and it was attempted on Monday evening or late afternoon. Yes. Towards the evening, yes. And that's how we did it. However, some ten kilometres from Dubica, on the road towards Sisak - because that was the only available road - I had to be transferred through Hrvatska Kostajnica and Bosanska Kostajnica into Bosnia. However, they caught me there and the driver who was taking me there, he and I were taken back. And then on Monday evening, I was locked into a special room in the old school building. I wasn't taken to the firehouse. And later on, I heard, once they started interrogating me, that there was nobody in the firehouse. Once we returned, four kilometres from Dubica near the river in Bacin, a grave was found with 43 persons who remained in the firehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this since I'm trying to find the explanation for all this: You said that you were arrested, they interrogated you, and then you were asked by the Prosecution whether you were beaten or not. You said that you were not. However, the topic of all this was to find out why you did not support the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They asked me about why I was detained there, why I was persecuted by the local authority, and they asked me why I did not accept to be the leader of the SDS and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I wrote down. You said that you were not beaten and that they interrogated you about the reasons for escaping from the firehouse and not accepting the position within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm referring to. Could we now there find a motive for detaining you there in the firehouse? Was it because of these party reasons, political party reasons? Do you have an explanation yourself for the fact that you were locked in the firehouse with other people, with 53 people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an explanation. I really don't know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew that there were Serbs and Croats and Muslims there with you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not detained on the basis of your ethnic origin but you think there was a political background to it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't know. We don't know why we were detained and locked in the firehouse. In fact, the guards told us that we had to wait because somebody was supposed to come and call a meeting. I don't know what the meeting was about. And this meeting never took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the meeting never took place while you were there until 6.00 p.m. and you don't know whether somebody came after 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you think that what you're saying about the parties appears to be specific of a multi-party system understood in the Balkan sense, that is, in the understanding of Hrvatska Dubica? Would you say that that provoked the problem that you encountered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say whether that was the reason or not, but I think that if it hadn't been for -- for that -- I don't know. If there hadn't been the SDS, the HDZ -- I can't answer that question. What caused it, I don't know. But until then, everything was fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about, Mr. C-1141. I also think that Yugoslavia, up till then, was, at least for me, the most beautiful country in the world.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: People were living in harmony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just saying what happened in my town. What happened afterwards, who ordered it, under whose control, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say that you know what happened to those people who stayed behind in the fire station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what basis can you say that and you don't know about other things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because the people who crossed the Una River on the Bosnian side are live witnesses. They heard shooting. And all those people were found there, exhumed and identified. What more do you want?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were those people exhumed and identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly; in 1996 or 1997. I don't know exactly when the exhumation was carried out. Afterwards, when we returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that this was a mass grave next to the river.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many bodies were exhumed at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All 43 that were identified. And there were others in the grave. I don't know how many. Because apparently they were brought there and executed there from other villages, from Crvljani. When they were brought there I don't know because they were not in the fire station while I was there. When they rounded them up, during the night or in the morning, I don't know. I don't know about the others. I just know that 43 persons from my town were sent away from the fire station and they're gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of page 5, at the end of the list, you say that the exhumation was carried out in March and April 1997 and 56 bodies were removed from the site. And out of those 56, 37 were identified, as well as many other villagers and your wife. "I was also present," you say, "when we identified a number of bodies."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. How could I identify bodies whether out of those 43 persons several persons couldn't be identified or their children didn't come who are someplace in Germany, Switzerland? They were not identified, but they were buried there. I and my wife couldn't recognise anyone because they were not our relatives. So don't ask me things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. C-1141, I'm not claiming anything that is not written in your statement. I'm just reading it out for you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Read it. Read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] "Our exhumation of the mass grave in Bacin took place Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in March and April 1997, and 56 bodies were removed from the site. Of those 56, 37 have been identified. Along with my other villagers and my wife, I was also present at the site when the exhumation took place, and we identified a number of bodies. Of those 43 detained at the fire station on 20th of October, the bodies of following persons were from Hrvatska Dubica." [Interpretation] And then you list 18 names, and first and last names. That is what is stated in your statement. I've read out every single word. Is that right or not? Is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my statement, but not that list. You don't have the real list. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know either, Mr. C-1141.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forty-three persons are on the list from my town who were killed, and out of the 43 of them, most were identified. I did not identify a single one, and I claimed that. And if you have something else written down there, I don't stand by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. C-1141, I don't have anything else in writing except what was given to me as your statement which you signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic was also given what is Prosecution Exhibit 344, the handwritten list of Mr. C-1141 and it contains a full list of the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, we have the point. We have the exhibit which the witness produced. Now, can move on to another point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just finish with this first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no dispute, even though you're saying this is not quite correct, there is no dispute that this was in March and April 1997, when the exhumation was carried out. That is what is stated in the statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1997, in the spring. I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. And you're claiming that they were killed in 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So six years prior to that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were buried on a river bank in a kind of collective grave; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well known where they were buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible, six years later, for you to recognise anyone six years later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I never claimed that I recognised anyone. The relatives, the relatives; my neighbours recognised their fathers. I didn't. How could I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that six years later people buried on a river bank in this humid earth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. C-1141, since you speak of the time you spent in the fire station, after that you were on the run, and you don't know anything that you are claiming that happened later that you didn't see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see. I was not with them. But there is no doubt. There is evidence. I didn't see it, but persons who were with me were found. I've explained. And when they caught me again, I learnt it then. That was on the Monday evening that I learned that they were no longer in the fire station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on Monday evening, you learned that there was no one in the fire station.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you conclude from that that they were taken away and killed then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that is the kind of conclusion you reach, could you at least intimate what could have been a motive for such a crazy act for some old men and women to be taken off and executed, people of different ethnicities and so on? What could have been the reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I'm surprised myself what could have been the reason and who could have ordered that, on whose authority and on whose will this was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could anyone gain from the killing of those people when there were no conflicts there even?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness has answered that he doesn't know, and he's as surprised as anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. C-1141, you are saying that you heard afterwards that those people were killed. You're not testifying about their killing because you don't know anything about it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I testify about the killing of that person when I wasn't there when they were killed? But there are live people who are alive who heard the screams and the shooting, and they identified the spot and reported that that is where they were buried, and they were found there. And dates are given, the time of day, the morning, when this happened, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to state that you are not testifying about this because you don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. I was with them and they are gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not disputed that you were in the fire station. But after that, you were on the run. After that, you were arrested, interrogated, and released again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What happened to me and how I happened to survive by chance, that's another matter. I was being sought after because I'm the only live witness of that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were not present.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Present at the killing? No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know anything about who committed that crime? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. And I keep asking myself why it was done and who did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know who did it nor why.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why it was done. This was an arbitrary killing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But who -- who did you learn about it from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From survivors and who were taken out during the week. I don't know how. Relatives. There's a waitress, a forestry worker. There is a list and they are alive, and they too are wondering why they killed them, why they didn't release everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are surprised and others. I, too, for instance, can wonder why those people were killed and who killed them. So you cannot answer the question who killed them nor why they killed them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it. If I knew who killed them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, is it disputed -- it may assist in clarifying the issues: Is it disputed that these 43 people who were -- whose bodies were exhumed were in fact killed in October 1991 as alleged? Is that fact in dispute?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I think it is absurd for you to ask such a question. How could I possibly know what happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... no, of course you don't know. But -- but at the end of this trial, we are going to have to make our minds up about events such as this, and we're going to have to make up our minds as to what occurred on the evidence which is produced. Now, the issues will be clarified if we know what is in dispute and what isn't. Now, you don't have to answer, of course, but in order to clarify, as I say, the issues and reduce them, it would be helpful to know if you dispute that this occurred or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, as you see also by the statement of the witness, it is inexplicable that something like that should have happened. And he doesn't know who could have done that. So that one could assume that those people died under different circumstances and not simply that they were brought to the fire station and after that executed. It is unbelievable this hypothesis that somebody should round up some old men and women in the fire station and then execute them. It is simply unbelievable. That's why my common sense says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be unbelievable, but the question is did it happen or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't doubt at all that this man is sincerely talking about what happened in the fire station. He described it. But what happened after that, he cannot know. He doesn't know. And he cannot claim something that he doesn't know. That is the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I lived through and what I saw I can assert, Mr. Milosevic. I don't understand why you're insisting so much on something that is not clear to you. And I told you that I don't know who killed them, but they were killed, killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-1141, you don't have to speculate as to that. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've got slightly under ten minutes more for questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. C-1141 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just on the transcript, what I said to the witness is you don't have to speculate as to that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not speaking about any speculations. I'm trying to establish, Mr. May, that the witness is not testifying about something he saw but about something that happened prior to that which may or may not point to such a course of events, and the course of events is so unbelievable that something like that should happen in a peaceful situation that the witness has told us about, I'm just asking what else could have been the cause for the death of these people. If they were exhumed and found dead six or seven years later, I assume that is true, and I'm not disputing that. What I'm trying to discover is what could have been the cause for the death of these people, because the explanation offered by the witness is simply unbelievable for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, Mr. C-1141, that there were Serbs, Croats, and Muslims there. Who were the people who were released, those ten who were released while you were there? Were they also of different ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then exclude as the possible reason any ethnic affiliation for the killing of these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both Serbs and Croats were killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only two Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The scale can be of significance, but nevertheless, both Serbs and Croats were killed. There's no dispute over that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there isn't any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then infer that this was not based on any kind of ethnic hatred? You, too, were arrested and you're a Serb.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could have been killed too.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that this was not any kind of ethnic hatred that prompted anyone to kill anyone else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're going to have to make that decision at the end of the case. The witness can merely tell us what he saw. What you can ask him -- I think you've probably covered it, but to make sure we'll cover it again: Could you see, Witness C-1141, any cause for this killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. I've thought about this, and I keep thinking about it, what the cause was. I think it was arbitrariness on the part of a group of people, several people. Why they did that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you indicate who these people were who took this arbitrary action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these people in my place, in my town. Whether they had received instructions from where else, I don't know, but those people were in my town. They're not there now. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you be more specific, please? You were asked a question about the brigade in your town. I intervened, and you said that there were 31 or 32 policemen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a brigade. Don't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I was claiming, that it wasn't a brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the police, and then there was a brigade or a battalion of the army. That was separate. That held the line from Jasenovac to Sunja along the Sava River. That's something else. They had a headquarters and a staff and a commander and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, you're saying that that was the line, a sort of front line. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that had nothing to do with the goings-on in your particular town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, very well. Now, these 31 or 32 policemen that you mentioned, they were your policemen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't my policemen. They were the police officers belonging to the militia, part of the local ones and some of the others I really don't know. I don't know where they came from but they all had patches on their shoulders saying Militia of SAO Krajina. And the vehicles had this written up on them too, the vehicles they used. It said the Police of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the fire station, were you guarded by the policemen, the Milicija or the local territorials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In that police uniform, the local ones were not wearing that uniform. I told you the type of uniforms they wore. But they were really reservists, at least, as far as I heard. Now, who they belonged to, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But these reservists were people who you knew. They were from your town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well let's just make a distinction between these two points: The police who arrested you afterwards and interrogated you afterwards didn't harm you at all, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't beat me. They were astonished. The person doing the interrogation was surprised why I had been accused. I asked who accused me and he didn't want to tell me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the policeman who arrested you was surprised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the one that interrogated you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was wearing civilian clothes. He was an inspector of some kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. An inspector in the police station. And he let you go, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't let me go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who let you go, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A group of those others did; the people, the locals, the young boys. They let me go and they let me go at night so that nobody else should know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, did the police do anything to harm you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except putting me in the fire station in the first place, because they knew -- their people had a list of names, and they went around the village collecting these people from the list, and they would call the names of the people out and take them to the fire station. Whenever they changed shifts, they would do the roll call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The roll call and the shift and guards in the fire station were not policemen but territorials; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Now, who they received their orders from, I don't know. They were probably linked up with the police. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's assume then that the police was not involved in this, that it was the territorials who were involved in all this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of them. These people guarded us and the other people brought us in. Both of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they might have had orders to bring people to a meeting. How do you know they didn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assumed that we were to have a meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Somebody must have said go and call these people to attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that's how it should have been, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we both agree on this assumption, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what does the police of Krajina has to do with what went on in the villages? And you still assume that it happened the way you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Krajina? I'm talking about the police force from my own local village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the -- your local police force then have to do with the events that took place later on? And you link up the reservists who are also from your place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that the reservists did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police gathered us all up, took us to the fire station, and we were guarded by the reservists. Now, who took them over later on I really don't know because I didn't see. And now let me tell you one other thing, Mr. Milosevic: Arbitrariness was prevalent 100 per cent. People did what they liked. All of them did. Now the person -- I don't know what name to give him, the person that was in charge of the policemen - not the army and reservists but in charge of the policemen - was on the run and his people had come into conflict with the police force of the Kostajnica municipality, and one of the policemen from the municipality of Kostajnica was killed. Now, why they had this conflict, because they wanted -- this man wanted to separate our region and an exit to Bosanska Dubica. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I know that you're talking about all this chaos that went on during the civil war when some local man wanted -- took it into his head to take your part of Bosanska Dubica and put it onto the other part. Now, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who ordered him to do this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we must be bringing this to a close because you've had the hour allotted and slightly more, but you can certainly ask two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. C-1141.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. This just shows how absurd it all is. You could have brought in any witness, a witness that had been on barley, to testify about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not listening to comments of that sort and you shouldn't be making them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: Do you live in Hrvatska Dubica today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this correct: That today in Dubica, of the 2.500 Serbs who lived there before the war, there are only some 30 remaining inhabitants; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Serbs were there before the war, how many are there now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were before the war. When it was a municipality, the number of inhabitants were 3.000 or closer to 4.000 inhabitants. Now, of that number, although I don't know exactly, but I would say that perhaps 50 per cent were Serbs. The ratio was 50/50 of Croats and Serbs. Now, today, in that place of ours, village of ours, there are many more Serbs living there than you have mentioned, and there are more and more every day, with each passing day. They've started coming back to their own homes, their own homes are being refurbished, but there are many more of them who are there today than the figure you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to go on with this cross-examination, you having had your time, Mr. Milosevic. Have the amici any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should just like to ask the witness for some explanations with respect to the document that has been tendered as an exhibit, along with the remark that I am not at all bringing into question the fact that all these persons did lose their lives. What I'm interested in is this, Mr. Witness: You said that the bodies were dug up from this mass grave in March and April 1997; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were dug up. Now, whether it was March or April, I really can't say, but it was in 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what you said in the statement you gave on the 3rd of August -- on the 8th of November, 2000, in fact.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested in this list, the list you have in front of you. When was it compiled? You made your statement to the Prosecution of the Tribunal in November 2000, but when was this list compiled? Because we can't see a date on it. Everything else is there but not the date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you the date right now. This list was copied out from the original list which I made in 1991 when I succeeded in leaving that prison again where I had spent two days and two nights. So once I left, that's when I made up the list. And I was transferred to Bosanska Dubica. I was there for several days, staying with friends, and that's when I compiled the list. Not this one but the list which was taken from me by the police. I don't know why they needed it. And I asked them to give it back to me. But what happened was this: They did not give the list back to me, and I sat down once again afterwards, and I sat down with my wife, and I know exactly, I know exactly who was from which house. Mostly -- there were six people from my own house, three men and six or seven women, older ones. And I know exactly where they were in the fire station, because three times in a single day, the list was read out. Three times a day. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I was asking you something else. So when did you actually compile this particular list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made this list up myself later on. It might have been in 1990 -- 2000, let's say. 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why isn't there a date on the list? That's what I'm asking you now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why isn't there a date?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I made this list up for myself so that I would have one, a copy. There is a date on the original, but the original was never given back to me. So why should I write the date down?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am asking this question for the following reason:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Prosecutor in November 2001, you said that you recognised only 19 persons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I have the list here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't recognise anybody. That's not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the following persons, bodies, were from Hrvatska Dubica, and you state -- you proceed to give 19 names and not 43.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You go ahead and try and remember, for example, when somebody asks you how many of us were at such-and-such a place. You try and remember. I wrote down my neighbours, the neighbours I knew about, but here we have people from the whole place, from the whole town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you did this on the basis your memory, your recollections, then you should have told the investigators of the Tribunal that. Did anybody dictate the list out to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, why would anybody dictate it out to me? I compiled the list myself. I sat there together with my wife and drew up this list, because she knew quite a lot of them. I knew some of them, but they were older people, and she knew more people than I did. I knew the younger ones. So it was I who compiled this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Re-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. C-1141, in response to a question of Mr. Milosevic, you said when you returned on the 2nd of October, you saw -- or you counted 12 houses that had been burnt by fire. And my question to you is: Did you know the owners of those 12 houses and can you please characterise for us were they a mixture of both Croat and Serb houses or one or the other ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly Croatian houses, but two houses were -- belonged to people who had mixed marriages; mine, the 13th one was set fire to, but later on. Not in October. It was set fire to later on, not then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it your understanding that the reservists, the men in military uniforms at the fire station, were under the command of this person you've described as Borojevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah. Well, I don't know that. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Borojevic, you said or you stated that he was not from Hrvatska Dubica. Did you ever have an opportunity to hear him speak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness C-1141, during the cross-examination by the accused, you once said like this, I quote: "But there are live people who are alive who heard the screams and the shooting, and they identified the spot and reported that that is where they were buried, and they were found there." Is that right? My question is --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- why could the exhumation not have taken place 2 earlier? It took place as late as in 1997, after the six years. But there was witnesses who can identify this place. Why couldn't that take place earlier? Could you make any observation on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. That was unclear to me as well, why not, because this was learnt about much before the time that they were exhumed and the spot pinpointed. Now, why this was not done, I really don't know. Why it wasn't done earlier, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Much has been made of the fact that the people taken to the police station comprised Croats, Serbs, and Muslims, and in response to the accused, at one time you said, in trying to explain that, "Arbitrariness was present 100 per cent." Would you like to elaborate on that? Are you suggesting that the action that took place took place in an arbitrary manner irrespective of the ethnic background of the persons who were subjected to that kind of treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they weren't taken to the police station but to the fire station. And second, why did this happen? It's not clear to me to this day. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you want to continue, continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1141 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, because up until then, there was no difference between us. Serbs, Croats, Muslims, we were all the same. We were there and we built up our town together, and it really is a little strange how somebody could have took it into their heads to -- or who could have come. Nobody knew him. He didn't recognise neighbours, anybody. And if he wanted to do something, why he didn't put them in a bus and take them away to Bosnia, for example, because in Bosnia it was peaceful at that time. And then from Bosnia, they could have crossed over to Croatia. I really don't know. It's not clear to me. But to collect them all up just like that and under the guise of taking them to a meeting which never took place. It was a Sunday, they didn't give us water or food the whole day, and in the evening, as I say, I saw that something was amiss, and I managed to get out. But the other people stayed there and they're not around any more. So quite certainly they didn't see the dawn of Monday morning. It was towards dawn that they were taken off and killed, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-1141, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we call the next witness, there is a matter I want to deal with in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has been granted the protection of pseudonym and facial distortion and will be known throughout the proceedings as C-060. In order to avoid his identification being revealed, I must ask for private session at certain places during his testimony, but principally to deal with matters of background which would be revealing of his identity. I would ask for a private session now and I will take those matters of background as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: C-060, we are concerned in your evidence principally with the area of the municipality of Podravska Slatina. It's in the north-east, as we'll see on a map shortly, of Western Slavonia, but before we move on to the evidence, just inform us, was Slatina ever taken control of by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to 1990, at elections in Slatina, did the SDP, led by Ivica Racan, win those elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you judge Racan to be a moderate or a man of extreme views?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: No. He was a moderate man. There was nothing based on which I could conclude he was an extremist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same election, the HDZ of Franjo Tudjman gained what percentage of the votes, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I think that at the level of the republic, they gained 30 per cent, and in our municipality, I suppose somewhere up to 30; perhaps 20 something per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 1991 census in Slatina revealed a division of ethnic groupings, I think with Croats amounting to what percentage and then tell us how many Serbs. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: When the census was conducted, there were 57 per cent of Croats in 1991, whereas Serbs constituted 34.5 per cent, and the rest were Yugoslavs, Hungarians, Czechs, and so on; they all made up about 8 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I turn to the SDS party in Western Slavonia. At the beginning of 1991, was there a man called Ilija Sasic who occupied a key position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall precisely what position he did hold?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he was a member of the Regional Board of the SDS for Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first president of the party in your own Podravska Slatina was whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: It was Mr. Milun Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did those two men relate one to the other? Was either the leader of the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes. Based on everything we saw, Mr. Karadzic in a way was manipulated by Mr. Sasic, Ilija Sasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ilija Sasic have a role in respect of volunteers? If so, what, and with whom did he contact? Volunteers and also armaments and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to explain that at the time, Mr. Ilija Sasic used to be a judge in the municipal court in Slatina, and then later on or in parallel with that, he was also politically active in the League of Communists. He was a member of leadership structures of the League of Communists in Slatina. And immediately thereafter, I think it was in 1990, he left the court and became an attorney, opened a private practice. And based on my experience, what I heard and in Slatina, in our local community and also later wider in Western Slavonia, he was associated to a great extent with the establishment of the SDS. And he was also quite well-connected to the leadership of that party. There was a lot of talk among the local population about the procurement of weapons. Prior to the units of the Territorial Defence being established, the name of Mr. Sasic was closely connected to the procurement of those illegal weapons and the establishment of those TO units. Based on what I know, Mr. Sasic contacted very influential people in Belgrade and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As a sign of his position generally, was there a time in April or May of 1991 when Goran Hadzic had been arrested by the Croatian police and negotiations were mounted to effect his release, with Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Sasic have any role to play in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sasic and Veljko Dzakula negotiated with Mr. Tudjman in respect of the release of these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 4, paragraph 7. You've mentioned Mr. Dzakula. How did his views as to a peaceable or otherwise solution to developing problems compare with those of Sasic? Was either of them connected to the man Seselj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Based on what I know, and I knew both of them, although I met Mr. Dzakula only in 1992, but based on the relations between those two, one could see that they were not supporting the same cause, namely, Mr. Sasic was more radical in organising Serbs and putting up resistance or, if I can say so, in the military sense, whereas Mr. Dzakula supported a proposition that was prior to that affirmed by late Dr. Raskovic. That was a peaceful solution, a democratic option that involved negotiating and negotiating ad infinitum. At least, that's how he presented this position to me. That was the difference between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the man Seselj ever seen in your area? If so, where and with whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes. In October of 1991 -- I can't, Your Honours, remember the exact time, but I'm sure it was either November or October of 1991, more likely November, so Mr. Seselj was accompanied by Mr. Vukelic, Sasic, and some other gentlemen, Bojcic, and I can't get -- say that -- those names. So they were in Vocin. I saw them in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Deal with the progress of the SDP party and the SDS party. In June of 1991, was there a decline in membership of the SDP party as members migrated in the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes. It is well known that in 1990, and this is usually pointed out, at first democratic elections in Croatia, HDZ won the majority on the republic level.
