That is the heading. And then it goes first, second, third paragraph, and the last sentence is the one that refers to a "mob."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't sign this text in this form. I signed it in English. Now, what the wording is in English, I don't know. Nor am I familiar with the English language. But I know the expressions I used and could have used, but there is an explanation for this particular wording.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the explanation, Mr. C-060?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: The explanation is that I know the people from my local community for 30 years, and I know very well which people I would like to be in a community of opinion with or a community of interests, members of my family and my close friends, and I also know which people I didn't want to associate with, and that's why I abandoned the party of which I was a member for 20 years. Those same people, individuals but a good number of them and a large proportion of the individuals had distorted, not such a bad idea, of Dr. Jovan Raskovic. Some of them were present at that convention. Neither then nor now nor in the future will I associate with them. However, I do not believe that I used this word "banda" or "mob," regardless of what it says here. I signed the statement in English, and these translations may be erroneous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I assume you made your statement in the Serbian language, not in English.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: When I made my statement, I was shown the text. I think the text was in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not given the text in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: It was given later. But I didn't - I don't know how to put it - go into that, because those were not things that I might hurt anyone's rights for me to go into details or any specifics, any details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I think the way you have described the Serbs in Croatia, that they are associated in a sort of mob, is not a question of punctuation, but I think it is a question of violation of rights. So I assume you would have reacted if you had a chance to do so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are attributing things to me in spite of what I have said. I did not say that my Serbs were a mob, but I said that some people behaved in a way that could be described as uncontrolled behaviour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. C-060, please bear in mind that I am not making any insinuations. I simply read out verbatim what is written in your statement which you yourself were able to see with your own eyes just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've dealt with that and he's given his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or, Mr. C-060, you can find the exact word you used in the English statement. I think you have that version. Could you find the word you used during your -- at the statement of yours. Or Mr. Nice could help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Does the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't -- through nobody's fault. We don't have the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact the word in the English statement is "mob. I've -- we've laid it before him, but I don't think he speaks English sufficiently necessary to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he didn't use the word. So we can't really take the matter very much further. The accused has read out the passage. Could we move on to something else, please, Mr. Milosevic. Perhaps you'd like to take the English back. Let the usher do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with that, when we're talking about your position, is it true, this reference to an incident that you provoked in the municipality building in Podravska Slatina, that you shot at the photograph of the late President Tito?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I never shot at anybody's picture and still less the picture of President Tito. And in Slatina, never in any public place did I use a weapon. In Slatina or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken into custody in connection with such an event, even if you were innocent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes, such an event was attributed to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this when you say this incident was attributed to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: That was in 1971.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1971, during the mass movement in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes. That coincided with that period. There was the "maspok" or mass movement in Croatia. That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was insinuated to you when you were arrested in 1971 in Croatia? What was it that you were charged with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: That I jeopardised the life of the chief of police and his employees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you do that in 1971?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I didn't, when he was lying. If I had, I would have been convicted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you were charged with at the time was not proven, or did they consider that the act did not merit a serious conviction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: No. The chief of police in Slatina and the police commander who made such a report were lying, and the investigating judge proved this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You say that in 1990 in Croatia, there was a significant percentage of the population who declared themselves to be Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes, there was quite a number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the members of which ethnic group mostly declared themselves to be Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Mostly people from mixed marriages. That is how we called it. Though some estimated that there were more Serbs. But I don't believe that. I don't know. Maybe that's true. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that in Podravska Slatina, you witnessed the Croats disassociating themselves from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did this occur already prior to the victory of the HDZ at the elections in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I would not be able to claim that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you're talking about the ethnic composition of the population of Podravska Slatina municipality, do you know what the situation was after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes, I was familiar with the data at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you no longer remembered them. To refresh your memory, perhaps you will remember, perhaps not; if you don't, tell me no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought he said he was familiar with the data. Go on. Put them to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the majority population were Serbs? 60 to 70 per cent Serbs, 30 per cent Croats. This was the situation -- 30 to 40 per cent Croats after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area in which you lived, Podravska Slatina. Do you know how the composition of the population in Podravska Slatina changed in the years following the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I come from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then tell me, do you know that by administrative decisions of the republican authorities of Croatia, several villages with a virtually hundred per cent Serbian population were attached to the municipality of Orahovica in which the Croats had a large majority, whereas, at the same time, some Croatian villages were attached to Podravska Slatina so that the Serbs in your municipality with these changes in the territories of the municipalities, the Serbs became a minority. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. I have a long memory of territorial and administration changes of local communities. In that context, this is also part of that. However, within the framework of the autonomy of those communities, I don't see any problem there in particular, especially since, as I said in my statement, we advocated brotherhood and unity in our part of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. What was the relationship between Serbs and Croats in 1991 in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I said that my statement; 57 to 35 per cent, and 8 per cent were the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that the municipality of Okucani, which was mostly Serb, through administrative measures by Croatia much earlier was divided into two parts, one part belonging to Novska with a majority Croat population and the other to Gradiska, again with a Croat majority, so that in both municipalities, as a result, the Serbs became the minority population by simply administrative decisions or paperwork. Do you remember that? Is that correct or are my data incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: No, that is quite true, only I don't see any particular reasons there. It was an autonomous decision of those people. If we're talking about historical decisions, one should ask Cedo Grbic; he's from Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not disputing that this occurred. The only thing is you don't know why the Croatian authorities undertook such administrative matters. That is something that you can't seem to find the reason for.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Actually, it was not just the Croatian authorities. There was the Croatian Serbian authority, at least while I was living there and where I was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. There is no dispute over that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I seem to have lost my pen, so can I borrow one from this gentleman next to me so as to be able to make some notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will go on, if we may, for another ten minutes if the interpreters will allow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in view of the fact that we've covered these questions concerning the elections and attitude of the Serb population towards political solutions in Croatia, the support for the SDP, et cetera, does it follow then that the Serbs in Croatia subsequently, more specifically in Podravska Slatina which you are testifying about and which you know best about, after the elections and at the end of 1991, as far as I can remember what you said, set up the SDS as a kind of response to the pressure, nationalist pressure that they were exposed to by the other side as a result of all these things that we have referred to coming from the HDZ, not only in the political and rhetorical sense but also dismissals, persecution, constitutional changes, et cetera, et cetera? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I didn't know, nor do I know with precision the motives to be able to tell them, but probably that one could assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But do you know, for instance, that a delegation of the SDS at that -- within the framework of the efforts to have all matters resolved by peaceful means, being aware of the problems that were cropping up under these pressures in the spring of 1991, in Zagreb, conducted talks with a group of some ten or so American congressmen? Among them was an American lady of Yugoslav extraction, Helen Delic Bentley, and also with the ambassadors of the USA, Germany, France, in Belgrade and presented to them the need for a peaceful resolution of the political situation in Croatia, familiarised them with the problems and sought their support for a peaceful settlement of what was known as the international community, support for a peaceful resolution of the problems in Croatia? Do you remember those initiatives, those efforts to ensure support, aid, protection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Dr. Raskovic's activities and the activities of other leaders of the SDS I had occasion to see only through the media in those days, and most frequently this was at the local level, that is, the media of the Republic of Croatia. In those days in 1991, I didn't have occasion to see any different approaches. And I don't remember noticing that they attended any such meeting, but I assume that they did, that one and others like it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in those delegations, that was not just one meeting, there was in Zagreb, in Belgrade, with there various groups, with congressmen and ambassadors and so on, do you know that Ilija Sasic was a member of this delegation, this man who you accuse rather grossly of selling weapons and warmongering? Do you remember that? Do you know that? He's a man from your environment, from your part of the country.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I do know of some media coverage given to Mr. Sasic within the framework of the SDS. I know more details about what I have testified about. I am not accusing him of anything except of what I heard from people in his circle and accusations made by them, and I have repeated them and made one myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let us make one thing clear, Mr. C-060. You didn't accuse him of anything that you are aware of personally but of only something that you heard from others who told you about it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: No. I knew a circle of people that he worked with, but I knew him personally. And judging from his statements, conduct, and meetings that I attended, I can assert with precision what I have said here regarding his positions and endeavours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that Ilija Sasic, with Franjo Tudjman, conducted negotiations in Zagreb to release Goran Hadzic. Are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I saw that in the media, and what I saw, if my memory does not fail me in these ten or 11 years, then that is what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in mid-March 1991 he negotiated with Tudjman but not prompted by this event but in connection with the release of some 30 Serb policemen that Croatian special forces had arrested in Pakrac without any combat and held them in custody in the Bjelovar prison? Do you know that that was what they discussed and not what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I remember this part in the media as it was presented, that it was Hadzic and Savic, I think. But I do allow for the possibility that policemen were involved as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that these Serbs were arrested and mistreated simply because they refused to put on their caps the chequerboard flag?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I don't know why, but I do know that the Croatian MUP punished them because of some kind of violation of a code. And this was an incident in March 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about March 1991. But tell me, then, the chequerboard flag, did it have the meaning of a political symbol for the Serbs or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I am a legalist, and I consider this to be an insignia of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia. Now, whether those people wanted or didn't want to accept it and to remain in service, I can't go into it. As to what Serbs think about it, I can't give you a collective answer. I can tell you what I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you probably have your own views - not offhand but with arguments - what Serbs think. Can you tell us how many thousand Serbs saw the chequerboard flag as the last thing they ever saw before dying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I only know that from history. Maybe better than you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am quite sure that you do, but do you think that their reactions were just some -- an expression of arrogance or was it in protest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I differ from some people in the expression of protests. A democratic option requires a different manifestation. However, this manifestation had its consequences, as you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that when Tudjman was engaged in these negotiations, that it was agreed that all problems should be resolved exclusively by peaceful means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I know that every time the agreement was to resolve questions by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that this peaceful resolution was unanimously accepted at a meeting of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party on the 30th of March, 1991, as a generalised model for dealing with the problems between Serbs and Croats in Croatia? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I probably heard of it, but I didn't follow the work of the SDS, and I cannot state emphatically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that already the next day, the 31st of March, 1991, on a Sunday, and this was on the 30th of March, Croatian elite forces attacked Serbs in Plitvice? The very next day. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I remember certain events. I don't know whether it was that particular date. I don't remember these details. It was outside my scope of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. C-060, do you know that on that very occasion during the attack that occurred after what you described, Goran Hadzic was arrested and not when you say and linking it to Sasic's negotiations with Tudjman? So it was only on the 31st of March during the attack on Plitvice that he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I assume that it was not properly interpreted. I was talking about negotiations about the release of Hadzic linked to the events in Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that even after this attack, Serbs advocated a peaceful solution to the crisis but that after all the negotiations, the Croatian authorities expressed and showed hypocrisy and continued their attacks on Serb villages and towns? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-060
utterances.text: I do know that the intervention of the Croatian police in certain areas in which the Serbs had a majority did represent a kind of provocation, but I also know that if we stick to legal forms of action by the authorities, this was part of their competence. Of course, I am not justifying their actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I've in fact cut the microphone off simply because it's time. It's 4.15, and we have to adjourn now. As far as tomorrow is concerned, we've decided that you should have up to two hours and a half cross-examination with this witness, which gives you one hour, 50 minutes tomorrow, should you want it. We shall be sitting tomorrow at half past nine to 4.15; and on Wednesday I should say we will be sitting from 9.00 until 1.00, adjourning at 1.00 precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I provided the summary of C-020 not to invite the Chamber to have to read it overnight because it will serve its purpose tomorrow but to deal with the point I made this morning about the need for private session which can probably be dealt with by looking at the headlines. The evidence will not be as long as the summary might suggest, for various reasons question which I'll go into tomorrow or demonstrate tomorrow. But the private session passage would in fact be everything from paragraph 7 to paragraph 43 because it's all one topic, as you'll see. So it's provided simply so that you can see in advance the problem we're advancing and how I've proposed to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll look at that. Witness C-060, would you be back, please, at half past nine tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
